results.title: Nebius Raises On-Demand GPU Prices Up to 21% From October 1: What an H100 Hour Now Costs | ServerCalc
highlights:
Nebius lifted pay-as-you-go GPU rates up to 21% on October 1 — H100 to $4.50 an hour, B300 to $9.50 — the second rise since spring as AI capacity sells out.

...

From October 1, 2026, Nebius raised its on-demand, pay-as-you-go rates across its four current Nvidia platforms. On its own published price list the per-GPU-hour numbers now read: H100 NVLink at $4.50, up from $3.85 (about 17%); H200 NVLink at $5.40, up from $4.50 (20%); B200 NVLink at $8.50, up from $7.15 (about 19%); and B300 NVLink at $9.50, up from $7.85 (21%). CPU-only servers were caught in the same round — the AMD EPYC Genoa vCPU now lists at $0.015 per CPU-hour, roughly a quarter more than before. Separately, from October 8 the provider moved preemptible capacity for these platforms onto dynamic spot pricing, so the cheap interruptible tier no longer has a fixed rate.

These are list prices for on-demand use. Committed and reserved terms are quoted separately and run well below the hourly rate; the increase lands hardest on buyers who pay by the hour with no commitment.

...

The hourly figures are small, but GPU servers run continuously and in multiples, so they add up fast. A single H100 left running around the clock for a 730-hour month now costs about $3,285 on demand, against roughly $2,810 before October 1 — close to $475 a month more for the same card. Nvidia's NVLink parts are usually taken eight to a node, and an 8×H100 box now runs $36 an hour, or about $26,280 a month flat out, up from near $22,480 — a jump of roughly $3,800 a month per node. On the newest silicon the numbers are larger again: a B300 is $9.50 an hour, so an eight-GPU B300 node is $76 an hour, more than $55,000 a month.

The longer trend is the sharper one. In early May the same H100 listed at $2.95 an hour; at $4.50 it is about 53% higher in roughly five months, and the B300 has moved from $6.10 to $9.50 over the same stretch. For a team that budgeted an H100 at spring rates, the single-card line has grown by more than $1,100 a month.

...

Nebius has not tied the increase to the cost of any one component. Its own executives have described a market where demand outruns supply: the company has said it sold capacity as fast as it could bring it online, and that it could sell its entire 2027 capacity on current deal terms. That is the same story driving the memory and storage shortages we have covered from the VPS side — capacity, power and advanced-packaging supply are the bottleneck, and when a provider cannot build fast enough, the on-demand price is the lever it pulls first. A hardware generation that is nominally faster per dollar does not help if you cannot get time on it at the old rate.

...

On-demand is now the most expensive way to run a steady AI load, and the gap to committed pricing is wide enough to change the decision. Treat the hourly rate as the price of flexibility: right for experiments, short fine-tuning runs, and bursty inference where idle time would otherwise be wasted. For anything that runs most of the month — production inference, long training jobs — a reserved or committed term, or spot capacity with checkpointing, is usually far cheaper per useful hour, and the premium for on-demand has only grown with this round.

results.title: Nebius raised H100 prices 17% and H200 prices 20% on September 17, effective October 1. H100 and H200 are two of the GPUs most teams rent for LLM training and inference. If … | Spheron Network
highlights:
Nebius raised H100 prices 17% and H200 prices 20% on September 17, effective October 1. H100 and H200 are two of the GPUs most teams rent for LLM training and inference. If you had an instance running under the old contract, the new rate applies to it now, not at renewal.

You did not choose that new rate. A fixed-term contract works like this: the provider sets a new price, and every running instance inherits it on the provider's schedule. Per-minute billing works differently. You pay whatever rate is posted right now, for the minutes you actually use, and nothing carries forward past that.

On Spheron, that means:

- You see the live rate before every deployment, not on an annual renewal notice.
- You can move a workload to a different GPU or provider the same day if a better rate shows up elsewhere.
- Reserved pricing still exists if you want a fixed rate locked in. On-demand just stays the default instead of something you have to opt into.

As of October 6, 2026, on-demand H100 starts at $2.01/hr on the marketplace, and spot H200 starts at $3.31/hr. Spot means the rate for using capacity that is free right now, and it runs below the on-demand rate. These are live marketplace numbers and can vary by region.

A fixed-term contract can raise your rate without warning. Check current on-demand and spot rates on the marketplace before your next renewal

highlights:
The NVIDIA B200 SXM moved from a median of $6.79 to $7.13 per GPU-hour week-over-week, a 4.9% increase, according to Ai Mining Co. observations. That single-SKU move carries meaningful implications for institutional buyers operating at scale, and this report examines exactly where that price sits across individual rental marketplaces and how wide the spread between them has become. The per-marketplace breakdown below documents current ask-side pricing, lot availability, and the gap between the lowest and highest quoted rates in active listings—a spread that, as AIMC data shows, is not narrow. Figures reflect the most recent weekly snapshot; readers should treat all values as point-in-time observations rather than continuous quotes.

Across the 14 marketplaces carrying B200 SXM this week, the observed median ranged from $3.69/hr at deepinfra to $8.19/hr at togetherai — a 2.2x spread between the lowest and highest median. Intra-SKU spreads of this magnitude reflect differences in commitment terms, regional availability, and how aggressively each provider is positioning the same hardware, rather than differences in the silicon itself. AIMC reports each marketplace's observed median independently and does not blend them into a single figure that would mask this dispersion — the spread itself is part of what the market is telling you.

...

The most striking feature of this week's B200 SXM data is not the aggregate price movement but the degree to which pricing fragments across the market. Ai Mining Co. tracked 14 active marketplaces quoting the B200 SXM this week, and the spread between the lowest and highest observed median was not marginal — it was structural. DeepInfra sat at $3.69 per unit while Together AI reached $8.19, a 2.2x differential across providers that are, in principle, offering access to the same underlying hardware. That kind of dispersion typically appears in markets where commitment structures, access tiers, or supply-side constraints differ meaningfully between providers — though the data alone cannot confirm which of those forces is dominant at any given marketplace. What the data does confirm is that a buyer landing on Together AI would pay more than twice what a buyer on DeepInfra pays for nominally equivalent capacity. That is a pricing environment where the choice of marketplace matters as much as, or arguably more than, any week-over-week price movement.

results.title: H100 and B200 Cloud GPU Hourly Rates: October 2026 Pricing Curve | SpecForge
highlights:
1. On-demand H100 80GB cloud rentals ranged $1.71 to $10.98 per GPU-hour across 52 tracked providers as of October 2026, with the cheapest listing at Gcore and a market median near $3.23.
2. Last-released GPUs (B200/B300/MI300X/RTX 5090) saw median prices climb from $2.12 to $4.72 per GPU-hour between October 2024 and September 2026.

...

Across 52 providers tracked on October 11, 2026, NVIDIA H100 80GB on-demand rentals spanned $1.71 per GPU-hour at Gcore to $10.98 at the top of the hyperscaler band, with a market median of $3.23 per GPU-hour and a separate H100 SXM listing from $2.27/hr [S1][S10].

Last-released GPUs (B200, B300, MI300X, RTX 5090) saw their on-demand median rise from $2.12 per GPU-hour in October 2024 to $4.72 in September 2026, while the Modern cohort (H100/H200/A100/L40S/RTX 4090/A10G/T4/L4) moved only $1.35 to $1.45 over the same window [S3].

...

GetDeploying's index of 5,225 listings across 85 providers put the cheapest H100 80GB listing at $1.71 per GPU-hour (Gcore on-demand), against a 12-month trend of +8% [S1]. Separately, the Silicon Data GPU Rental Index recorded an isolated H100 spike of +10% in four weeks, from $2.00/hr on December 9, 2025 to $2.20/hr on January 6, 2026, with A100 and B200 flat over the same window [S5].

That spike ran counter to a multi-year normalization: H100 hourly rates fell from roughly $8/hr in early 2024 to a $1.50-$3.00/hr range by late 2025 across specialist providers, and H100 lead times compressed from over 50 weeks in 2023 to shorter delivery windows in 2024 [S5]. The October 2026 cross-provider range of $1.71 to $10.98 per GPU-hour now straddles both the discount end (boutique clouds, neoclouds, marketplace hosts) and the premium hyperscaler tier [S1][S4].

...

The Blackwell generation carries a steep premium: B200 180GB lists from $3.75 per GPU-hour at Packet.ai with a $6.69 median, B300 288GB starts at $4.99 with a $7.87 median, and GB200 186GB starts at $10.50 with a $16.00 median across five providers [S1][S3]. The Grace Blackwell Ultra GB300 288GB tops the table at $18.00 per GPU-hour on Oracle Cloud, and Vast.ai's October 2026 live snapshot shows B200 at a $6.00 floor and $7.50 median, with H200 NVL at $3.71/$4.25 and H200 at $4.37/$5.00 [S1][S6].

Reserved versus on-demand spreads are GPU-specific: B300's reserved median is $5.71 against $7.87 on-demand, H100 has a tight $0.13 gap ($3.10 reserved vs $3.23 on-demand), and MI300X actually inverts the pattern, with reserved at $3.39 above its $2.91 on-demand median [S3]. For engineering procurement, the on-demand column is the safe reference; reserved medians combine mixed commitment terms and cannot be read as a same-provider discount [S3].

...

Four variables move the hourly rate more than anything else. (1) Chip generation: B-series Blackwell cards cost 2-3x the H100 median, and the Grace Blackwell modules (GB200/GB300) add another 1.5-2x on top [S1]. (2) VRAM and HBM tier: 80GB HBM3 H100 lists cheaper than 141GB HBM3e H200 in many markets, but the H200's $4.40 median is justified by bandwidth for LLM inference [S3]. (3) Provider class: hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, GCP) cluster at the high end, with Azure H200 at $13.78/hr, while neoclouds and marketplaces (Vast.ai, Gcore, Beam) anchor the floor [S1][S3]. (4) Billing tier: spot rates sit below on-demand, but spot capacity is unreliable for long jobs [S3].

results.title: Alexey Gubarev: Why Compute Stopped Getting Cheaper
highlights:
## What GPU rental prices are really saying

At first glance, rental rates look like a counter-argument. According to the price tracker Silicon Data, H100 rates fell from around $8 an hour in early 2024 to between $1.50 and $3.00 by late 2025. Look more closely, though. The fall has stopped: Silicon Data's H100 index jumped 10% between early December and early January, its biggest short-term move since mid-2025.

And the same chip rents for roughly $1.90 an hour from specialist providers and more than $4 from the largest clouds. A twofold spread on identical silicon means customers aren't paying for the chip. They're paying for guaranteed capacity, in a building with power, close to the rest of their systems.

results.title: GPU Rental Prices Explained: On-Demand, Spot, Reserved, and Hidden Costs | flatkey.ai
highlights:
The short version: compare cost per completed workload hour, not only GPU price per clock hour.

## The quick GPU rental prices framework

Start every GPU rental prices comparison with one normalized formula:

```
effective GPU cost per completed workload =
  (GPU compute + storage + snapshots + bandwidth + idle time + retries + support + engineering overhead)
  / completed training, inference, batch, or media job units

```

...

| Provider or market | Official pricing source to check | What to capture | Notes for comparison |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vast.ai | Vast.ai pricing and Vast.ai FAQ | GPU model, host reliability, interruptible status, storage, bandwidth, verification tier, datacenter or community host | Vast.ai GPU rental prices are marketplace-driven, so two RTX 4090 or H100 offers can differ by location, host, reliability, storage, and network. |
| RunPod | RunPod pricing and RunPod storage and network volume docs | Secure Cloud vs Community Cloud, GPU model, pod storage, network volume, serverless worker pricing, idle time | RunPod GPU rental prices vary by cloud type and product mode. Compare pods, serverless, and storage separately. |
| Massed Compute | Massed Compute pricing | On-demand hourly GPU rate, long-term reservation or cluster quote, GPU memory, region, support scope | Massed Compute GPU rental prices are useful to benchmark dedicated AI cloud capacity, but private or reserved clusters may need a quote. |
| Lambda Cloud | Lambda Cloud pricing | On-demand GPU instance, GPU count, local storage, region availability, reserved cluster terms | Lambda publishes simple hourly GPU cloud rates for common NVIDIA instances; confirm current availability before planning a time-sensitive run. |
| AWS EC2 | Amazon EC2 pricing and EC2 Spot Instances | Instance family, region, On-Demand, Spot, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, EBS, data transfer, support | AWS is often the reference model for on-demand, spot, and committed-use economics, but GPU instance families and regional availability matter. |
| Google Cloud | Compute Engine GPU pricing and Spot VMs | GPU type, machine family, region, Spot VM status, committed use discount, persistent disk, network egress | Google Cloud separates GPU, machine, disk, network, and discount mechanics. Normalize all of them before comparing to specialist GPU clouds.

...

On-demand GPU rental prices are the cleanest starting point: you pay for the GPU capacity while the instance, pod, or server is running, usually with no long-term commitment. This is the mode most teams should use for first benchmarks because it keeps engineering variables simple.

On-demand is usually the right default when:

...

- You need provider support and predictable networking more than the lowest hourly rate.

The risk is idle time.
